hook: The world’s smallest porpoise lives nowhere else.

story.text: A vaquita surfaces without spectacle: a small grey back, a dark ring around each eye, then water again.
This porpoise lives only in the northern Gulf of California.
Its entire known world is a narrow reach of sea between desert coasts, where sound and touch matter more than sight.
Vaquitas navigate and find food by echolocation, sharing the water with fishing communities whose lives are also bound to the gulf.
The danger is not that vaquitas are hunted.
They become entangled in gillnets, including illegal nets set for totoaba, and cannot return to the surface to breathe.
Research reported by NOAA found no evidence that inbreeding alone makes recovery impossible.
The hopeful condition is also the difficult one: deaths in gillnets must stop.
To witness the vaquita is to remember that disappearance is not abstract.
It is shaped by choices—how fishing is supported, how illegal wildlife trade is confronted, and whether protection in one small sea is made real.

generalizedRange: Temperate forests of the Russian Far East and northeast China
hook: The world’s rarest big cat wears a winter coat.

story.text: Not many people ever see an Amur leopard. It is a cat of deep forest and far distances, awake mostly at night.
It lives and hunts alone in the vast temperate forests of the Russian Far East and northeast China.
Winter is written into its body. In the coldest months, the hairs of its black-ringed coat grow up to seven centimetres long, and its long furred tail wraps around it for warmth.
For decades it was hunted mercilessly, while logging, forest fires, road building and farming broke its homeland into fragments.
It remains one of the rarest and most endangered leopard subspecies in the world.
And yet the recent story bends toward hope: research shows conservation work is having an effect, and wild numbers are believed to be rising in Russia and China.
To witness the Amur leopard is to hold both truths at once—how close the edge came, and how much a protected forest can still return.

generalizedRange: Predator-free island and fenced sanctuaries, New Zealand
hook: The world’s heaviest parrot cannot fly—and booms in the dark.

story.text: The kākāpō answers almost every expectation of a parrot with an exception. It cannot fly. It walks the night with an owl-like face and a waddling gait.
It is the heaviest parrot in the world, and possibly the longest-lived bird, with lives measured in many decades.
It is also the world’s only lek-breeding parrot: in breeding years, males boom across the hills for nights on end.
Kākāpō are taonga—a treasured species—to Ngāi Tahu, the principal Māori iwi of southern New Zealand.
Once found across New Zealand, kākāpō nearly vanished after human arrival brought hunting, habitat loss, and predators their ground-nesting lives could not survive.
Every kākāpō alive today lives wild on predator-free islands or in fenced sanctuaries, watched over by the Kākāpō Recovery programme.
Its keepers contend with low hatching success and the constant need for more predator-free habitat—and still the population has grown.
To witness the kākāpō is to learn how much care a species can require, and receive.

generalizedRange: Canals of Xochimilco, southern Mexico City, Mexico
hook: The salamander that never grows up lives in one city’s canals.

story.text: The axolotl is a salamander that refused to grow up, and made a life of it.
Unlike other salamanders, it is neotenic: it keeps its larval body—feathery external gills, a swimming tail, a fin along the body—for its entire life, and never leaves the water.
It descends from tiger salamanders and has lived in central Mexico for perhaps ten thousand years.
Its world was once a great basin of lakes and wetlands—Xochimilco and Chalco—along the southern edge of the Valley of Mexico.
Most of that water was drained as Mexico City grew, and wild axolotls now survive in a few isolated sites in the city’s south.
The axolotl is woven deep into Mexican history, culture, and identity, and it is famous in science for regrowing what it loses.
Yet fame has not protected the water it needs. Its remaining habitat is small, isolated, and hemmed in by one of the world’s largest cities.
To witness the axolotl is to see that a species can be everywhere in culture and almost nowhere in the wild.

generalizedRange: North America, overwintering in central Mexico and coastal California
hook: A migration measured in generations is growing thin.

story.text: The monarch is the rare wild animal almost everyone has met: an orange-and-black butterfly drifting through a summer garden.
More than beautiful, monarchs are pollinators—while feeding on nectar they pollinate many kinds of wildflowers.
Their caterpillars, though, eat one thing. Monarchs must lay their eggs on milkweed.
Each autumn, monarchs east of the Rockies fly to overwinter in the mountains of central Mexico, while western monarchs gather at sites on the California coast.
No single butterfly makes the whole journey. The migration is completed across generations.
Once abundant across North America, monarchs are now in decline, pressed by habitat loss, pesticides, and a changing climate.
Their recovery is unusually close to home: milkweed native to your region, nectar flowers from spring through fall, and gardens managed without pesticides.
To witness the monarch is to notice that even a common wonder can thin—and that a backyard can be part of the answer.

action.title: Plant native milkweed
action.summary: Use the Xerces Society’s regional guides to plant milkweed native to your area and nectar flowers that bloom spring through fall—and skip the pesticides.
